weeks.title: Talking with God: Prayer
weeks.theme: Prayer is a conversation between God’s children and their Father—not a ritual, but a relationship.
group: How did you pray before, or what did you think prayer was?
Which line of the Lord’s Prayer moves you most?
What could you practice praying about this week?
weeks.guide: Many new believers feel, “I don’t know how to pray,” or “my prayers aren’t spiritual enough.” Model simple, honest, everyday prayer, and let them know prayer is just talking with the Father. You can teach a simple shape like the Lord’s Prayer: praise, confession, thanks, requests. Pray together at least once this week and let them speak too; afterward say gently, “See? You can pray.” Also introduce the 321 online gatherings—morning reading, noon devotion, evening prayer—so they can pray with a community.
weeks.meet: This week, pray with the person walking with you: each share one thing you are thankful for and one need, then pray for each other.
weeks.keyText: In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.

lessons.title: The Father in Secret
text: But you, when you pray, enter into your inner room, and having shut your door, pray to your Father who is in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly.
In praying, don’t use vain repetitions as the Gentiles do; for they think that they will be heard for their much speaking.
Therefore don’t be like them, for your Father knows what things you need before you ask him.
lessons.hear:
Many people think prayer needs beautiful words, long hours or special postures, so they find it hard and simply stop. In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus made prayer very simple and very personal: “But you, when you pray, enter into your inner room, and having shut your door, pray to your Father who is in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will reward you openly” (Matthew 6:6).

An “inner room” with the door shut is a quiet place without interruptions and without performance. Prayer isn’t spoken for people to hear; it is spoken to the Father. Jesus continues: “In praying, don’t use vain repetitions as the Gentiles do… for your Father knows what things you need before you ask him” (Matthew 6:7-8).

If the Father already knows, why pray? Because prayer isn’t giving God information; it is building a relationship. Children tell their parents about their day; parents already know much of it, yet still love to hear. Prayer is your conversation with the Father: you can give thanks, complain, cry, ask—just be honest.
lessons.light: Prayer is relationship, not ritual. The relationship with God comes before every other relationship. Live by the heart through the Spirit: prayer isn’t assembling fine sentences in your head, but speaking to the Father from your heart.
think: What made prayer hard for you before?
“The Father already knows, yet loves to hear you”—how does that change your praying?
Where and when could your “inner room” be?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for seeing and hearing me in secret. I don’t need fancy words; I just want to talk with you like a child. Teach me to pray, and let prayer become my favorite time each day. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Find an “inner room” today (a bedroom, your car, a park bench). Close the door (or put on headphones) and spend five minutes telling the Father about your day.
lessons.quick: Prayer isn’t a performance—it’s talking heart to heart with the Father.

lessons.title: The Prayer Jesus Taught
text: Pray like this: “‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy.
Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
Give us today our daily bread.
Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.
Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. For yours is the Kingdom, the power, and the glory forever. Amen.’
lessons.hear:
The disciples saw Jesus praying often and asked him, “Lord, teach us to pray” (Luke 11:1). Jesus gave them a model, the Lord’s Prayer: “Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy. Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven. Give us today our daily bread. Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one” (Matthew 6:9-13).

The prayer has a beautiful order: God first, then us. First honoring God’s name, asking for his kingdom and his will; then asking for daily bread, forgiveness and protection. Our needs aren’t unimportant, but when God is at the center, our needs find their proper place.

You can use the Lord’s Prayer as a “frame” and add your own words after each line. For example, after “Let your will be done on earth,” you might say: “Lord, at my work and in my home, let your will be done.” Praying this way, prayer isn’t just a long list of requests, but includes praise, surrender, trust and forgiveness.
lessons.light: The heart of the Lord’s Prayer is letting Jesus reign and letting God receive all the glory: “Let your Kingdom come.” Building God’s order means letting the Lord’s Prayer be fulfilled in our lives: his will done on earth as in heaven.
think: Which line of the Lord’s Prayer is easiest for you to pray? Which is hardest?
What does the order “God first, then us” remind you about your usual prayers?
“Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors”—is there someone you need to forgive?
lessons.speak: Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy. Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven. Give us today our daily bread. Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Use each line of the Lord’s Prayer as a frame, add a sentence or two of your own after each, and pray it slowly once.
lessons.quick: Seek God’s kingdom first, then bring my needs.

lessons.title: Pray About Everything
text: In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.
And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.
lessons.hear:
Modern life is full of worry: work pressure, finances, health, children, the future. When Paul wrote this, he was in prison—worse off than us—yet he said: “In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God” (Philippians 4:6).

“In nothing be anxious” doesn’t mean pretending everything is fine; it tells you where to put your worries. It’s like hiking with a heavy backpack when someone says, “Put the pack in the truck—it’s going up too.” Worry is the backpack; prayer is putting it in the truck. Notice Paul says “in everything”—not only big things: a parking space, an exam, a coworker, a child’s fever.

The result? “And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:7). The problem may not be solved right away, but the heart receives peace first. This peace “surpasses all understanding”—even you find it strange: nothing has improved yet, so why am I so calm? That is God guarding you.
lessons.light: Worry often comes from “I need to control this”; prayer hands control to God. Handing burdens to God is letting God be God and people be people. When our focus moves from the problem to Jesus, peace comes.
think: What is your biggest worry right now?
You can pray about “everything.” Do you pray about small things?
Have you experienced “peace that surpasses all understanding”?
lessons.speak: Father, I hand you my worry: ___. I don’t want to carry it alone anymore; I put it in your hands. Thank you that you will guard my heart and my thoughts. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: List three things that worry you. Hand each to God in one sentence, and write one thing you are thankful for beside each.
lessons.quick: Turn worry into prayer, and God’s peace guards your heart.

lessons.title: Thankful Prayer
text: Always rejoice.
Pray without ceasing.
In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you.
lessons.hear:
A psychologist once ran an experiment: one group wrote down three things they were thankful for each day. After a few weeks they were happier, healthier and slept better than the other group. What science discovered, the Bible already said: “Always rejoice. Pray without ceasing. In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you” (1 Thessalonians 5:16-18).

“In everything give thanks” doesn’t mean everything is good; it means we can find God’s grace in everything. Giving thanks when ill isn’t thanking God for illness, but for his presence in it; giving thanks in failure isn’t thanking him for failure, but because God can work all things together for good. Gratitude is a pair of glasses: put them on and you can see God’s hand in ordinary, even difficult, days.

“Pray without ceasing” doesn’t mean kneeling twenty-four hours a day. It means talking with God anytime, like breathing: waiting in line, walking, washing dishes. “Thank you, Lord” or “Lord, help me” are prayers too. Let prayer be not only a slot in your day but the background music of the whole day.
lessons.light: Giving thanks in everything gives glory to Jesus: all is God’s grace. A thankful heart overcomes a complaining heart, just as humility overcomes pride. Complainers see what is missing; the thankful see God.
think: What three things can you thank God for today?
In something bad, what can you still find to be thankful for?
At what moments in your day could you practice “praying without ceasing”?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for today: thank you for ___, ___ and ___. Even where things went wrong, I believe you are with me. Help me always rejoice, pray without ceasing, and give thanks in everything. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Starting today, for seven days in a row, write down three things you are thankful for before bed.
lessons.quick: Gratitude is a pair of glasses that shows God in ordinary days.

lessons.title: Speak, Your Servant Hears
text: The LORD called Samuel again the third time. He arose and went to Eli and said, “Here I am; for you called me.” Eli perceived that the LORD had called the child.
Therefore Eli said to Samuel, “Go, lie down. It shall be, if he calls you, that you shall say, ‘Speak, LORD; for your servant hears.’” So Samuel went and lay down in his place.
The LORD came, and stood, and called as at other times, “Samuel! Samuel!” Then Samuel said, “Speak; for your servant hears.”
lessons.hear:
Young Samuel lived in the temple. One night he heard someone call his name and thought it was the old priest Eli. He ran to him: “Here I am; for you called me.” Eli said, “I didn’t call you.” This happened three times before Eli realized God was calling the boy. He taught Samuel: “If he calls you, … you shall say, ‘Speak, LORD; for your servant hears’” (1 Samuel 3:9).

Prayer isn’t only us speaking; it includes listening to God. Many people’s prayers are like phone calls where they talk and hang up without waiting for a reply. Does God speak? Yes. He speaks mainly through the Bible, and also through the Holy Spirit’s promptings in our hearts, through circumstances, and through mature believers. But we need to learn to be still and listen.

This week we learned about prayer: talking with the Father in secret, praying the Lord’s Prayer, handing worries to God, giving thanks in everything, and listening quietly. Prayer is like breathing—a basic skill of spiritual life. Next week we learn another basic skill: reading the Bible, eating spiritual food.
lessons.light: Listening is humility: “Speak, your servant hears” admits that God knows better than I do. The Holy Spirit is my guide; his voice is often gentle, and we must be still to hear it.
think: Is your prayer more “speaking” or “listening”?
In what ways do you think God has spoken to you?
How can you make a little room for “listening” in your life?
lessons.speak: Lord, speak; your servant hears. I talk a lot but rarely listen quietly to you. Teach me to be still, so I can hear you speak through the Bible and through your Spirit. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: When you pray today, after you finish speaking, be quiet for three minutes. Say to God, “Speak—I’m listening,” and write down what comes to mind.
lessons.quick: Prayer is a conversation: speaking to God and listening to him.

weeks.title: Hearing God: Reading the Bible
weeks.theme: The Bible is spiritual food and a lamp to our feet; hearing and doing it roots our life.
group: When and how did you read the Bible this week? What was hard?
Which of “See, Hear, Think, Speak, Do” helped you most?
Which verse did you recently put into practice?
weeks.guide: Helping a new believer build a Bible-reading habit matters more than teaching lots of information. This week, read a passage together using “See, Hear, Think, Speak, Do,” then let them lead you through one. Suggested order: Mark → John → Acts → Philippians → Genesis. Encourage them to use the app’s highlighting, reflections and Bible Fun, and remind them: not understanding is fine—write down questions and discuss them when you meet.
weeks.meet: This week, agree with the person walking with you to read the same passage (e.g., Mark 5) and share the sentence each of you highlighted when you meet.
weeks.keyText: Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.

lessons.title: Spiritual Food
text: But he answered, “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth.’”
lessons.hear:
Someone who goes three days without eating becomes desperately hungry, yet someone who goes three months without God’s word may feel nothing at all. That doesn’t mean the spirit needs no food; it means the spirit has grown numb with hunger. After Jesus fasted forty days in the wilderness, the devil tempted him to turn stones into bread. Jesus answered: “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth” (Matthew 4:4).

The body needs food; spiritual life needs God’s word. A baby needs milk every day, not one big feeding a month; a new believer also needs a little of God’s word each day—not a lot, but consistently. Peter says: “as newborn babies, long for the pure spiritual milk, that with it you may grow” (1 Peter 2:2).

Many say, “I’m too busy to read the Bible.” But however busy we are, we still eat. It isn’t lack of time; it’s that we haven’t yet treated it as a “meal.” Try treating Bible reading like breakfast: it doesn’t have to be a feast—a short passage, ten minutes—but eat every day.
lessons.light: Live by the heart through the Spirit: Bible reading isn’t accumulating knowledge but nourishing life. Life first, then living: for life to grow, it must eat God’s word daily.
think: Is your spirit well fed, hungry, or numb with hunger?
Which ten minutes each day could you use to “eat” God’s word?
What usually steals your Bible-reading time?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you said we don’t live by bread alone but by every word from God’s mouth. I admit I often leave my spirit hungry. Give me a hunger for your word, so I eat spiritual food every day. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Set a daily phone reminder for Bible reading (in Settings or your reading plan), and read a passage of Mark today.
lessons.quick: The body eats every day; so must the spirit.

lessons.title: A Lamp to My Feet
text: Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.
lessons.hear:
People who walked at night long ago carried an oil lamp. It didn’t shine far—just a step or two ahead—but that was enough to keep walking without stumbling. The psalmist says: “Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path” (Psalm 119:105).

God’s word may not show you the whole blueprint of your life at once, but it lights up your next step. Should I change jobs? How do I handle conflict? What do I do when my child rebels? The Bible may not give a direct answer, but it gives principles and light: honesty, forgiveness, humility, trust, loving your neighbor. Decisions made in that light are less likely to go astray.

This is what 321 means by “the Bible is my standard.” The world has many voices: the internet, trends, friends, our own feelings. They change and sometimes contradict each other. God’s word is a steady standard, like a ruler that can measure the other voices. When you face a choice, first ask: “What does the Bible say?”
lessons.light: The Bible is my standard. I don’t judge the Bible by my feelings; I let the Bible correct my feelings. Move from a human perspective to God’s perspective, from the world’s view to the Bible’s view.
think: What are you facing that needs light for the next step?
When you make decisions, whose voice do you usually listen to most?
In what area of your life does “the Bible is my standard” most need practice?
lessons.speak: God, your word is a lamp to my feet. I don’t need to see the whole road at once; just light my next step. Help me ask what your word says in every decision. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Think of a decision you are facing, find a related verse (ask Xiaozhi or the person walking with you), write it down, and carry it in prayer.
lessons.quick: God’s word may not light the whole road, but it lights the next step.

lessons.title: Hear It, Then Do It
text: But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.
For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man looking at his natural face in a mirror;
for he sees himself, and goes away, and immediately forgets what kind of man he was.
But he who looks into the perfect law of freedom and continues, not being a hearer who forgets but a doer of the work, this man will be blessed in what he does.
lessons.hear:
Imagine someone looking in a mirror and seeing a smudge on his face. He looks, walks away and does nothing. What good is the mirror? James says those who hear the word without doing it are like that: “For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man looking at his natural face in a mirror; for he sees himself, and goes away, and immediately forgets what kind of man he was” (James 1:23-24).

James says: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves” (James 1:22). The biggest danger in Bible reading isn’t failing to understand, but understanding and not doing. Knowing a lot without changing can even make us proud, as if knowing were the same as doing.

So the last step of Bible reading is always “do.” It doesn’t need to be big—one concrete small step: a gentle word to family today, praying for someone, not complaining once, repaying a debt. James promises that the doer “will be blessed in what he does” (James 1:25). When God’s word is lived out, it truly enters our life.
lessons.light: The eight steps of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Practice, Review, Adjustment, Repetition, Multiplication. Many stop at “Information”—hearing much but practicing little. Moving from hearing to doing is how a mindset truly changes a life.
think: Have you read or heard a lot without actually doing it?
The last time you did something because of the Bible, what happened?
What concrete small step can you take from today’s passage?
lessons.speak: God, I don’t want to be only a hearer, deceiving myself. Help me do what I hear, so your word becomes real change in my life. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Look back at the “Do” steps of the past few weeks. Pick one you haven’t done yet and finish it today.
lessons.quick: The last step of reading the Bible is always “do.”

lessons.title: Meditating Day and Night
text: Blessed is the man who doesn’t walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand on the path of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers;
but his delight is in the LORD’s law. On his law he meditates day and night.
He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither. Whatever he does shall prosper.
lessons.hear:
Psalm 1 describes a blessed person: “his delight is in the LORD’s law. On his law he meditates day and night. He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither. Whatever he does shall prosper” (Psalm 1:2-3).

The word “meditate” carries the sense of murmuring something over and over, like a cow chewing its cud—chewing what it swallowed again and again to draw out all the nourishment. Reading the Bible isn’t only reading through; it’s keeping one sentence in your heart and chewing on it all day: while driving, washing dishes, before sleep. That is meditation.

A tree planted by streams looks like any other tree—until drought comes. Other trees wither, but its leaves stay green, because its roots reach the water. Life has dry seasons too; those whose roots go into God’s word in ordinary days still have life in hard times. This isn’t done in a day or two; it comes from planting and watering every day.
lessons.light: Everything we do flows from the heart. Meditation lets God’s word drop from the head into the heart, from information into revelation. A heart open to God finds joy; a mind left to itself finds worry: chew on God’s word, and the heart is renewed.
think: Is there a verse that has stayed in your heart these past weeks?
What would “a tree planted by streams of water” look like in your life?
At what time of day could you practice meditating on one verse?
lessons.speak: God, I want to be like a tree planted by streams of water. Help me delight in your word and meditate on it day and night, so my roots reach into your word and I don’t wither in drought. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Choose one verse (for example, Psalm 1:3) and say it at least three times today at different times, asking what it says to you.
lessons.quick: Meditation is chewing on one word from God all day long.

lessons.title: See, Hear, Think, Speak, Do
text: This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it; for then you shall make your way prosperous, and then you shall have good success.
lessons.hear:
After Moses died, Joshua had to lead a whole nation into the Promised Land. It was a huge task and he must have been afraid. God didn’t say, “Study more military strategy.” He said: “This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it; for then you shall make your way prosperous, and then you shall have good success” (Joshua 1:8).

Notice three actions: “not depart from your mouth” (say it often), “meditate on it day and night” (reflect), and “observe to do” (practice). This is exactly the structure of each lesson in this app: See (read the text), Hear (hear it explained), Think (reflect), Speak (talk to God in prayer), Do (practice). You have learned this way for fourteen weeks!

Today’s step is to make this method your own. You don’t have to use this app—just a Bible and a notebook. Each day read a passage and write: What did God say to me today? What do I want to say to God? How will I live it out? When Bible reading moves from “taking a course” to “meeting God myself,” your spiritual life truly takes root.
lessons.light: The Bible is my standard and the place I meet God. “See, Hear, Think, Speak, Do” is changing our mindset in practice: Information (see), Revelation (hear), Conviction (think), Prayer (speak), Practice (do). Repeat it and life is changed.
think: Which of the five steps do you most often skip?
Do you feel ready to “meet God yourself”?
Which book of the Bible do you want to read next month?
lessons.speak: God, thank you for teaching me to read your word with “See, Hear, Think, Speak, Do.” I want to meet you every day—not just to study a course, but to build a relationship with you. Make my way prosperous. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Tomorrow morning, without opening the course, read a short passage of Mark yourself and write five lines of notes using “See, Hear, Think, Speak, Do.”
lessons.quick: See, Hear, Think, Speak, Do—let Bible reading become meeting God.

weeks.title: The Holy Spirit: Presence and Guidance
weeks.theme: The Holy Spirit lives in believers—comforting, guiding and changing us so we bear the life of Christ.
group: Had you heard of the “Holy Spirit” before? Any impressions or worries?
Have you ever sensed a gentle prompting inside?
Of the nine fruits of the Spirit, which do you long for most?
weeks.guide: New believers often hold one of two extreme pictures of the Holy Spirit: very mysterious and frightening, or only about special experiences. Help them understand that the Spirit is a person, God himself, the Counselor (companion, helper), who lives in every believer; his main work is making us more like Jesus and bearing the fruit of life. Don’t compare spiritual experiences or dismiss their feelings—bring the focus back to Jesus and the Bible.
weeks.meet: This week, read Galatians 5:22-23 with the person walking with you. Each choose the fruit you most want to grow in, and pray for each other.
weeks.keyText: I will pray to the Father, and he will give you another Counselor, that he may be with you forever: the Spirit of truth, whom the world can’t receive, for it doesn’t see him and doesn’t know him. You know him, for he lives with you and will be in you.

lessons.title: Another Counselor
text: I will pray to the Father, and he will give you another Counselor, that he may be with you forever:
the Spirit of truth, whom the world can’t receive, for it doesn’t see him and doesn’t know him. You know him, for he lives with you and will be in you.
lessons.hear:
On the night before Jesus left his disciples, they were deeply troubled. For three years Jesus had been beside them; when he left, what would they do? Jesus comforted them: “I will pray to the Father, and he will give you another Counselor, that he may be with you forever: the Spirit of truth” (John 14:16-17).

“Counselor” means “the one called alongside”—it can be translated comforter, advisor, helper, advocate, like a coach, friend or lawyer always at your side. Jesus said “another,” meaning one just like himself. When Jesus was on earth he could be with people in only one place; when the Spirit came, he could live in the heart of every believer.

Jesus also said: “he lives with you and will be in you” (John 14:17). This is one of the most wonderful truths of faith: God isn’t only in heaven or only in church; he lives in you. You are never alone. When you are lonely, weak, or don’t know what to do, the Counselor is in you.
lessons.light: The Holy Spirit is my guide. He isn’t an energy but God, living in the heart. Everything we do flows from the heart, because the Spirit lives in the heart, not in the head.
think: Of the meanings of “Counselor,” which do you need most right now?
“God lives in you”—do you believe it? How does it make you feel?
Have you sensed God’s presence when you were lonely?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for sending the Counselor, the Holy Spirit, to be with me forever and live in me. I am never alone. Holy Spirit, comfort me, guide me and help me. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Today, at a moment when you feel lonely or tense, say in your heart: “Holy Spirit, thank you for being with me.”
lessons.quick: I am never alone—the Counselor lives in me.

lessons.title: You Are God’s Temple
text: Or don’t you know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God? You are not your own,
for you were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God’s.
lessons.hear:
In Old Testament times, God’s presence dwelt in the temple. People went to the temple in Jerusalem to worship, and its holiest place, the Most Holy Place, was entered only by the high priest once a year. In the New Testament, Paul says something astonishing: “Or don’t you know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God?” (1 Corinthians 6:19).

Your body is God’s temple! This gives the body great dignity. It isn’t that only the “spirit” matters and the body doesn’t; nor can the body do whatever it likes. Paul continues: “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God’s” (1 Corinthians 6:19-20).

This affects how we treat our bodies: eating, sleep, exercise, sex, addictions. Not binding ourselves with rules, but caring for this temple with respect. You are not your own; you were bought back by Jesus at the cost of his life, and your body is where God lives. Seeing yourself this way, you won’t despise yourself or misuse yourself.
lessons.light: “You are not your own”—this is the truth of selflessness: my body and my life belong to God. It isn’t losing freedom but the dignity of being bought at a great price. Glorifying God in our bodies is letting Jesus reign in our daily life.
think: How does “my body is a temple of the Holy Spirit” change how you see your body?
Is there a habit you need to see anew as “caring for the temple”?
What does “you were bought with a price” mean to you?
lessons.speak: Lord, thank you for buying me back at a great price and making my body a temple of the Holy Spirit. I want to glorify you in my body. Help me care well for the place where you live. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Choose one small change to care for your body (sleep earlier, one fewer sugary drink, a ten-minute walk) and start today as thanks to God.
lessons.quick: My body is where God lives—glorify God in it.

lessons.title: Led by the Spirit
text: For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.
lessons.hear:
Paul says: “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God” (Romans 8:14). Being led by the Spirit is a mark of God’s children. But how does the Spirit lead us? Usually not with a loud voice from heaven, but in gentle ways.

First, the Spirit leads through the Bible. He is its author, and his leading never contradicts it. Second, the Spirit prompts within. You may have experienced this: about to say something hurtful, a voice inside says “don’t”; seeing someone in need, something nudges you “go help.” That is often the Spirit. Third, the Spirit leads through peace. When we follow God’s heart, there is peace inside; when we drift, there is unease.

Learning to be led by the Spirit is like learning to recognize a good friend’s tone of voice; it takes time and practice. Obey one small prompting, and the next will be easier to hear. 321 says, “The Holy Spirit is my guide,” and “only the selfless can be led by the Spirit.” When we stop insisting on our own way, the Spirit’s voice becomes clear.
lessons.light: Only the selfless can be led by the Spirit. The self-centered can’t hear the Spirit because their own voice is too loud; the selfless lay themselves down, and the Spirit’s gentle voice becomes clear. Live by the heart through the Spirit, not by the head through yourself.
think: Have you experienced a gentle prompting or nudge inside?
Of the three ways the Spirit leads, which is most familiar to you?
When is “your own voice” loudest, drowning out the Spirit?
lessons.speak: Holy Spirit, please lead me. I often insist on my own way and can’t hear your voice. I am willing to lay myself down and obey your promptings. Help me recognize your voice more and more. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Today, when you sense a prompting to “do good” or “not do wrong,” obey it right away once, and write down tonight what happened.
lessons.quick: Only a selfless heart can hear the Spirit’s gentle voice.

lessons.title: The Fruit of the Spirit
text: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith,
gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.
lessons.hear:
An apple tree doesn’t strain to squeeze out apples. As long as its roots are in the soil and its branches are connected, apples come in their season. Paul says: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22-23).

Notice: it is “fruit,” not “works”; it is “of the Spirit,” not produced by our effort. These nine qualities are really the character of Jesus. When the Spirit lives in us, his main work is making us more and more like Jesus. Not by gritting our teeth to become loving and patient, but by staying connected to Jesus, so that his life flows out of us.

321 calls this “920”: everyone connected to you is your “2”; in each relationship, practicing the selfless “0” bears the nine fruits, the “9.” These fruits are most tested in relationships: patience with family, gentleness with coworkers, peace in conflict. Relationships are the orchard where the Spirit bears fruit.
lessons.light: 920: every relationship is a 2; practice the selfless 0; bear the 9 fruits of the Spirit. Fruit isn’t squeezed out—it comes from connection; the more connected to Jesus, the more we live out Christ’s life in relationships.
think: Of the nine fruits, which is most evident in you now? Which is most lacking?
What is the difference between “bearing fruit” and “doing work”?
Which relationship in your life most needs the fruit of the Spirit?
lessons.speak: Holy Spirit, I long to bear your fruit. I admit I often lack ___ (for example, patience). I don’t want only to grit my teeth; help me stay connected to Jesus so your life flows out of me. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Choose the fruit you need most and deliberately practice it once today in a specific relationship (for example, listening patiently until a family member finishes).
lessons.quick: Fruit isn’t squeezed out—it grows from staying connected to Jesus.

lessons.title: Walking by the Spirit
text: But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.
If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.
lessons.hear:
Paul says: “But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh” (Galatians 5:16). “Flesh” here doesn’t mean the body but the old self-centered nature. Inside a believer it feels like two forces pulling: the old self that wants to be in charge and satisfy itself, and the Spirit who wants us to be like Jesus.

There’s an old illustration: two dogs are fighting inside you, a black one and a white one. Which one wins? The one you feed. Prayer, Bible reading, worship and being with spiritual companions feed the life of the Spirit; indulgence, complaining, addiction and isolation feed the old flesh.

Paul says: “If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit” (Galatians 5:25). “Walk” here carries the sense of keeping in step, following the leader’s pace step by step. We don’t arrive at the finish all at once; we keep in step with the Spirit every day. This week we met the Holy Spirit: he is the Counselor, lives in us, leads us and makes us bear fruit. Next week we face challenges on the road of faith: temptation, doubt and family opposition.
lessons.light: The old self-centered life and the new selfless life pull against each other. Walking by the Spirit is the selfless overcoming the self-centered. Live by the heart through the Spirit, not by the head through yourself: relying on ourselves we fail; relying on the Spirit we overcome.
think: Lately, which of your “two dogs” has been stronger?
What do you do regularly that feeds the life of the Spirit?
How can you begin keeping in step with the Spirit today?
lessons.speak: Holy Spirit, I want to walk by you. I admit I often feed my old self, so it is strong. Help me choose to feed the new life and keep in step with you every day. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: List the three things you spend the most time on each day. Ask: which “dog” do they feed? Make one small adjustment.
lessons.quick: The one you feed is the one that wins.

weeks.title: Facing Temptation, Doubt and Family
weeks.theme: The road of faith brings temptation, doubt and family misunderstanding, but God is faithful and will make a way of escape.
group: Since believing (or seeking), what has been your biggest challenge?
How has your family reacted to your faith?
How can you both respect your family and hold on to your faith?
weeks.guide: This week matters a lot. Many new believers now meet family opposition (especially around folk worship and ancestor rites), temptation from old habits, and low points of faith. Ask proactively: “Does your family know you believe in Jesus? How did they react?” Help them respond to family with respect, wisdom and gentleness—neither clashing head-on nor hiding their faith to avoid conflict. For ancestor-rite questions, see the Questions tab and encourage them to witness through doubled filial care. If conflict is serious or safety is at risk, bring a pastor alongside.
weeks.meet: This week, talk honestly with the person walking with you: where are you most often tempted? How does your family view your faith? Pray for your family together.
weeks.keyText: No temptation has taken you except what is common to man. God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted above what you are able, but will with the temptation also make the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.

lessons.title: When Temptation Comes
text: No temptation has taken you except what is common to man. God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted above what you are able, but will with the temptation also make the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.
lessons.hear:
Believing doesn’t mean there will be no more temptation; sometimes it becomes more noticeable. Before, doing wrong didn’t bother you; now your heart feels uneasy and you struggle. That isn’t bad—it shows the new life inside you is alive. Paul offers great comfort: “No temptation has taken you except what is common to man. God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted above what you are able, but will with the temptation also make the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it” (1 Corinthians 10:13).

This verse holds three pieces of good news. First, you aren’t the only one: others have faced your temptation. Second, God sets a limit: he won’t let temptation exceed what you can bear. Third, there is always a way out: God will make one.

The way of escape is often very practical: leave the situation, close the website, don’t meet alone, call a spiritual companion, delete that number. Often “running away” is the most spiritual action. When Joseph was seduced by his master’s wife, he left his cloak and ran. Facing temptation isn’t a contest of willpower; it’s about who finds God’s way of escape fastest.
lessons.light: The self-centered think they can handle temptation, and fall again and again. The humble admit weakness, know how to flee and ask for help. Humility overcomes pride—and temptation too.
think: What temptation do you face most often? When are you most likely to fall?
“Running away is the most spiritual action”—what do you think?
What might the “way of escape” God has prepared for you be?
lessons.speak: Faithful God, thank you that you won’t let me be tempted beyond what I can bear. I admit I am weak in ___. When temptation comes, show me the way of escape you have made, and give me courage to take it. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: For your most common temptation, plan a “way of escape” ahead of time (a concrete action), write it down, and tell a spiritual companion you trust.
lessons.quick: Facing temptation isn’t a contest of will—it’s finding the way out fastest.

lessons.title: How Jesus Overcame Temptation
text: Again, the devil took him to an exceedingly high mountain, and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory.
He said to him, “I will give you all of these things, if you will fall down and worship me.”
Then Jesus said to him, “Get behind me, Satan! For it is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and you shall serve him only.’”
lessons.hear:
When Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, the devil took him to a very high mountain, showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, and said, “I will give you all of these things, if you will fall down and worship me.” It was the temptation of a shortcut: gain the whole world without going to the cross.

Jesus answered: “Get behind me, Satan! For it is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and you shall serve him only’” (Matthew 4:10). Three temptations, and three times Jesus answered, “It is written.” He didn’t debate the devil or rely on his own strength; he used God’s word.

This gives us a very practical weapon: store Scripture in your heart. When the voice says “you don’t deserve love,” answer with Romans 5:8; when it says “you can’t make it alone,” answer with John 14:16; when temptation says “just this once,” answer with 1 Corinthians 10:13. That’s why each week has a memory verse: they are your spiritual weapons.
lessons.light: Satan’s greatest temptation is to get people to worship self instead of God, taking a shortcut to glory. Jesus refused and let God be God. Selflessness overcomes Satan: when we stop grabbing for glory, Satan’s temptations lose their power.
think: Is there a “shortcut” temptation in your life?
Jesus said “It is written” three times. What does that teach you?
How many of the memory verses from past weeks do you remember?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for overcoming temptation for me. Help me store your word in my heart, so that when temptation comes I too can say, “It is written.” I will worship the Lord my God and serve him only. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Review past memory verses. Choose the three that help you most and save them in your phone notes as your “spiritual armory.”
lessons.quick: Jesus overcame with “It is written”—so can I.

lessons.title: When Doubt Knocks
text: But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all liberally and without reproach, and it will be given to him.
But let him ask in faith, without any doubting, for he who doubts is like a wave of the sea, driven by the wind and tossed.
lessons.hear:
After believing, doubts may return: “Does God really exist?” “Am I being naïve?” “If God loves me, why am I still suffering?” Many think having doubts means their faith is bad, so they don’t dare voice them—and doubt grows bigger in the dark.

James says: “But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all liberally and without reproach, and it will be given to him” (James 1:5). God gives “without reproach”; you can bring your questions to him. Doubt itself isn’t sin; it can become a chance to know God more deeply. Many people of great faith—Job, David, Thomas—went through deep doubt.

Some good ways to face doubt: first, say it—tell the person walking with you or tell God in prayer; second, look for answers—faith can withstand questions, so read, research and ask experienced people; third, remember what God has done, and keep a record of his work in your life; fourth, keep walking—even when feelings fade, keep reading, praying and gathering, and feelings often return. Faith isn’t the absence of doubt; it is choosing to trust even with doubts.
lessons.light: Hiding doubt is pride (afraid others will see my weakness); bringing doubt to God is humility. The humble admit “I lack wisdom,” and God gives generously.
think: What doubts have you had recently? How do you usually handle them?
“God gives without reproach”—how does that make you feel?
Is there something God has done in your life that can be an anchor when you doubt?
lessons.speak: God who gives generously without reproach, I have some doubts in my heart: ___. I don’t want to hide them; I bring them to you. Give me wisdom, and help me trust you even in my doubt. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Start a “Grace Journal” (you can use the app’s notes): write three things God has done in your life. Read it when doubt comes.
lessons.quick: Faith isn’t the absence of doubt—it’s trusting even with doubts.

lessons.title: When Family Doesn’t Understand
text: But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear,
having a good conscience. Thus, while you are spoken against as evildoers, they may be disappointed who curse your good way of life in Christ.
lessons.hear:
For many Chinese seekers and new believers, the hardest part isn’t intellectual questions but family opposition: “You’re following a foreign religion—don’t you care about your ancestors?” “Who will honor us after we die?” “You’ve been brainwashed!” Facing a family’s misunderstanding is painful and puts you in a hard place.

Peter wrote to believers facing opposition: “But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear” (1 Peter 3:15). Notice the attitude: humility and respect. Not winning an argument with your family, but explaining with a gentle attitude and a respectful heart.

He continues: “having a good conscience. Thus, while you are spoken against as evildoers, they may be disappointed who curse your good way of life in Christ” (1 Peter 3:16). Families are often persuaded in the end not by good arguments, but by seeing your change: a better temper, more filial care, more willingness to share housework. Your life is the first Bible your family will read.
lessons.light: Pride provokes pride: clashing head-on with family only hurts both sides. Humility brings out humility: responding with gentleness and respect, letting a changed life speak, can lead to a win for both. People matter more than winning arguments.
think: How has your family reacted to your faith? How do you feel about it?
How do you usually respond to your family’s challenges—gently?
What change can your family see in you?
lessons.speak: Lord, my family doesn’t yet understand my faith. Sometimes I am sad and torn. Give me a gentle and respectful heart—not arguing, but witnessing with my life. I pray for my family too, that one day they will know you. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: This week, do something kind for your family that surprises them (wash the dishes unasked, have a meal with your parents, call to check in). Don’t mention faith—just show love.
lessons.quick: My life is the first Bible my family will read.

lessons.title: Honoring Parents, Following the Lord
text: Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right.
“Honor your father and mother,” which is the first commandment with a promise:
“that it may be well with you, and you may live long on the earth.”
lessons.hear:
Many worry: “If I believe in Jesus, will I be unfilial?” In fact, the Bible values honoring parents highly. The fifth of the Ten Commandments is “Honor your father and mother.” Paul says: “‘Honor your father and mother,’ which is the first commandment with a promise: ‘that it may be well with you, and you may live long on the earth’” (Ephesians 6:2-3). In God’s eyes, honoring parents isn’t optional; it brings blessing.

What about ancestor worship? Christians don’t bow to ancestor tablets—not because they don’t love their ancestors, but because worship belongs to God alone. That doesn’t mean not remembering ancestors. Christians can express filial love in other ways: visiting and cleaning graves at Qingming, bringing flowers, telling ancestors’ stories, thanking God for their kindness, and giving their all at family gatherings. Many Christians actually care for their parents more attentively, come home more often, and carry more family responsibility—letting their families see that those who believe in Jesus are more filial.

Stage four ends here. Over these four weeks you learned prayer and Bible reading, met the Holy Spirit, and learned to face temptation, doubt and family. These are lessons in putting down roots in God’s love. In the next stage, we prepare for something important: baptism, publicly declaring to the world that you follow Jesus.
lessons.light: Let God be God: worship belongs to God alone. Let people be people: honoring parents is God’s command. The two don’t conflict; each has its place. Living out doubled filial love is how our lives give Jesus glory.
think: What do you think of the claim “believing in Jesus makes you unfilial”?
In what ways can you express filial love to parents and ancestors?
What kind of filial love do you hope your family will see in you?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for valuing honor toward parents. Help me honor my parents more than before, loving them in ways they understand. Give me wisdom so that, while worship is for you alone, my family still feels my love and respect. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Call or visit your parents (or an elder) and thank them, naming one specific thing they have done for you.
lessons.quick: Those who believe in Jesus should be more filial, not less.
